```{r setup, include=FALSE}

library(jsonlite)

summary_data <- fromJSON("central_american_republics_summary_cache.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
sett_data <- fromJSON("central_american_republics_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)

clean_label <- function(x) {
  s <- as.character(x)
  s <- gsub("&", "and", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("\\\\", "", s)
  trimws(s)
}

clean_hgis_source <- function(src, country) {
  s <- trimws(as.character(src))
  if (grepl("Davidson", s, fixed = TRUE)) return("INE Honduras; Davidson (2002)")
  if (identical(country, "Guatemala")) return("INE Guatemala (2018)")
  if (identical(country, "El Salvador")) return("DIGESTYC / BCR-ONEC (2024)")
  if (identical(country, "Honduras")) return("INE Honduras (2013)")
  if (identical(country, "Nicaragua")) return("INIDE Nicaragua (2005)")
  if (identical(country, "Costa Rica")) return("INEC Costa Rica (2022)")
  if (identical(country, "Panama")) return("INEC Panamá (2023)")
  if (identical(country, "Belize")) return("SIB Belize (2022)")
  s
}

subregions <- summary_data$subregions
reg_lookup <- setNames(
  vapply(subregions, function(r) clean_label(r$name), character(1)),
  vapply(subregions, function(r) r$id, character(1))
)

tot_area <- as.numeric(summary_data$area_km2)
tot_1830 <- as.numeric(summary_data$domain_trajectory[["1830"]])
tot_1900 <- as.numeric(summary_data$domain_trajectory[["1900"]])

n_sett <- as.integer(summary_data$settlement_stats$total_settlements)
n_suburbs <- as.integer(summary_data$settlement_stats$suburb_count)
```

# Abstract

Between the declaration of Central American independence from Spain in September 1821 and the close of the first quarter of the twenty-first century in 2025, the human population of the Central American isthmus from Guatemala and Belize to Panama multiplied roughly fortyfold. Across eight territorial sub-regions covering a harmonised raster footprint of 587.326 km², aggregate population expanded from 1,17M (1.171.449) in 1830 to 3,40M in 1900, 9,19M in 1950, 21,01M in 1980, 34,72M in 2000 and 45,27M (45.268.077) in 2025, closely tracking twenty-first-century national census benchmarks across Guatemala (14,90M in 2018), Honduras (8,30M in 2013), El Salvador (6,03M in 2024), Nicaragua (5,14M in 2005), Costa Rica (5,04M in 2022), Panama (4,06M in 2023) and Belize (397,5k in 2022) [@INEGuatemala2019; @INEHonduras2015; @DIGESTYC2024; @INIDENicaragua2006; @INECCostaRica2023; @INECPanama2023; @SIBBelize2024]. The political geography of that expansion was repeatedly reshaped by nineteenth-century border realignments, export monocultures and interoceanic transit corridors: the brief Federal Republic of Central America (1823 to 1841), the transfer of Chiapas to Mexico in 1824, the rise of highland coffee republics in Guatemala, El Salvador and Costa Rica, West Indian labour immigration into Caribbean banana enclaves from Limón and Bocas del Toro to Colón, Tela and La Ceiba, Panama's 1903 separation from Colombia, the establishment and 1979 reversion of the United States Panama Canal Zone (62,8k inhabitants in 1912 easing to 44,2k in 1970) and the 1970 relocation of British Honduras's capital from hurricane-struck Belize City to inland Belmopan prior to Belizean independence in 1981 [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @JaenSuarez1978; @USCensusCanalZone1973; @PerezBrignoli2010]. After 1950, falling infant mortality unleashed a prolonged demographic surge that fractured into sharply divergent national trajectories: Costa Rica and Panama completed early fertility transitions and entered demographic ageing, Guatemala and Honduras retained high rural fertility far longer, and El Salvador, Nicaragua and Guatemala endured acute civil-war mortality and mass emigration during the 1970s and 1980s [@Glei2019Costa; @B2009Presentacion; @Acevedo2024Emigration; @Rosas1988Mortalidad; @Rosas1988Mortalidadb]. Pairing national and sub-national census registers with a 469-settlement urban gazetteer spanning city-proper cores, 17 independent metropolitan suburban municipalities and historic Canal Zone townships, this study reconciles the modern demographic evolution of the entire isthmus [@Maria2017Central].

# Background

## Dissolution of the Kingdom of Guatemala and the Federal Republic (1821 to 1841)

When Central America declared independence from Spain on 15 September 1821, the former Captaincy General of Guatemala was a sparsely peopled agrarian bridge linking New Spain to New Granada. Roughly 1,28M people lived between the Maya highlands of western Guatemala and the Darién forests of Panama, strung overwhelmingly along the volcanic Pacific piedmont and intermontane basins while the humid Caribbean lowlands remained thinly settled forest and mangrove swamp [@HallPerezBrignoli2003]. Within months of independence, political unity fractured along both external and internal seams. Following brief annexation to Agustín de Iturbide's Mexican Empire (1822 to 1823), the five core provinces formed the Federal Republic of Central America in July 1823, yet Chiapas chose permanent incorporation into Mexico in 1824 (followed later by the Soconusco district), detaching an entire highland Maya demographic belt from the isthmian state system [@HallPerezBrignoli2003]. Meanwhile, the Isthmus of Panama remained attached to Gran Colombia and subsequently the Republic of New Granada (later Colombia), tying its nineteenth-century demography to South American administrative registers even as its transit economy served Atlantic-Pacific maritime commerce [@JaenSuarez1978]. On the northeastern Caribbean coast, the British woodcutting settlement along the Belize River operated outside Spanish republican jurisdiction, evolving formally into the Crown Colony of British Honduras in 1862 [@SIBBelize2024].

Inside the Federal Republic, provincial rivalries between conservative landed elites in Guatemala City and Granada and liberal factions in San Salvador, León and Tegucigalpa triggered recurring civil wars from 1826 to 1841. Wartime levies, disrupted overland trade and the devastating cholera epidemic of 1837 checked natural increase across the middle decades of the nineteenth century [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @PerezBrignoli2010]. Even after the federation dissolved into five sovereign republics between 1838 and 1841, demographic momentum stayed sluggish. In the harmonised JAGUAR regional trajectory, aggregate population across the eight sub-regions edged from 1,17M in 1830 to 1,25M in 1840 and dipped briefly to 1,21M in 1850 before climbing past 1,43M in 1880 and 1,52M in 1890. Early republican capitals remained modest provincial towns: Ciudad de Guatemala stood at 32k in 1825 and 40k in 1850, León at 25k and Granada at 15k in 1850, San Salvador at 16,5k in 1830, San José at 16k in 1844, Managua at 12k in 1850, Ciudad de Panamá at 11k in 1851, Tegucigalpa at 10k in 1850 and Belize City at barely 4,5k in 1832 [@INEGuatemala2019; @DIGESTYC2024; @INECCostaRica2023; @INECPanama2023; @SIBBelize2024].

## Nineteenth-Century Coffee Republics and Agrarian Transformation

Demographic stagnation broke during the last third of the nineteenth century as global industrial demand drew Central America into export agriculture. Coffee transformed the volcanic highlands and western slopes of Costa Rica, El Salvador and Guatemala first, followed more slowly by the north-central hills of Nicaragua [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @PerezBrignoli2010]. Costa Rica pioneered the shift out of its isolated Central Valley (*Meseta Central*), where smallholder and medium-sized family estates expanded steadily around San José, Heredia, Alajuela and Cartago. Steady export revenues financed basic sanitation, road linkages to Puntarenas and later Puerto Limón, and the earliest sustained national census series on the isthmus beginning in 1864, lifting Costa Rica from roughly 62k inhabitants at independence to 243,2k by the 1892 census [@INECCostaRica2023; @PerezBrignoli2010].

In El Salvador and Guatemala, coffee expansion operated under far tighter land concentration and coercive labour regimes. Salvadoran liberal governments abolished communal indigenous *ejidos* and *tierras comunales* in 1881 and 1882, converting the fertile slopes around Santa Ana, Sonsonate, La Libertad and San Salvador into dense commercial coffee belts [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Gomez2017Extranjero]. Because El Salvador possessed no empty Caribbean frontier, rural population packed tightly onto its compact 21.240 km² territory, driving national numbers from roughly 248k in 1821 to 703,5k by 1892 and laying the structural foundation for the highest population density on the American mainland [@DIGESTYC2024]. In Guatemala, the liberal revolution of 1871 similarly mobilised highland Maya labour from Huehuetenango, Quiché, Totonicapán, San Marcos and Alta Verapaz toward Pacific piedmont (*Boca Costa*) and Verapaz coffee plantations through debt peonage and vagrancy laws, while German merchant-planters anchored Cobán's regional rise (18,4k by 1880). Guatemala reached 1,36M inhabitants in its 1893 census, retaining demographic primacy across the isthmus [@INEGuatemala2019]. Honduras, fractured by rugged cordilleras and lacking a dominant volcanic coffee core, grew more gradually from roughly 155k in 1821 to 331,9k in 1887 and roughly 400k in the 1895 territorial census analysed by Davidson, before silver mining around Tegucigalpa and northern coastal banana concessions reordered its spatial balance [@Davidson2002; @INEHonduras2015].

## Caribbean Banana Enclaves and West Indian Migration

Until the 1870s, the Caribbean littoral of Central America from Belize to Darién remained demographically marginal, held loosely by Miskito, Garifuna, Creole and Afro-indigenous coastal communities alongside scattered timber camps. Between 1875 and 1930, railway construction and United States fruit companies—chiefly United Fruit and Standard Fruit—created a chain of export banana enclaves that permanently altered the ethnic and spatial demography of the Atlantic slope [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Zabaleta2013Mercados]. Because highland mestizo and indigenous workers resisted seasonal descent into malaria- and yellow-fever-ridden tropical lowlands, railway contractors and plantation managers recruited tens of thousands of English-speaking Afro-Caribbean labourers from Jamaica, Barbados, Saint Lucia, Grenada and the Cayman Islands [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Grugni2015Exploring].

This West Indian migration built new port cities almost from scratch along the Atlantic arc. In Costa Rica, construction of the Atlantic railway from the Central Valley to the coast turned Limón from an uninhabited anchorage into a thriving Afro-Caribbean port (2,1k in 1892, 7,6k in 1927, 11,3k in 1950 and 65,3k by 2020) [@INECCostaRica2023; @PerezBrignoli2010]. Across the border in northwestern Panama, Bocas del Toro (Changuinola and Almirante) drew parallel waves of Jamaican and Barbadian workers into banana plantations, while Colón—founded as Aspinwall in 1850 at the Atlantic terminus of the Panama Railroad—surged from 1,5k in 1855 and 6,5k in 1885 to 17,7k in 1911 and 31,2k in 1920 [@JaenSuarez1978; @INECPanama2023]. On the north coast of Honduras, banana railways radiating inland along the Sula and Aguán valleys propelled San Pedro Sula from a tiny village of 3,4k in 1887 to 17,5k in 1930 and eventually Honduras's industrial engine (701,2k in 2023), flanked by the coastal ports of La Ceiba (4,6k in 1910 to 209k in 2023), Tela and Puerto Cortés [@INEHonduras2015; @Davidson2002]. Guatemala opened Puerto Barrios in 1895 as its Caribbean railhead (4,2k in 1921 to 100,6k in 2018), while Nicaragua's Caribbean port of Bluefields (4,7k in 1906) and later Puerto Cabezas anchored timber and banana exports along the former Mosquito Reserve [@INEGuatemala2019; @INIDENicaragua2006]. During the Great Depression of the 1930s, however, Panama disease (*Fusarium* wilt), falling fruit prices and exclusionary nationality laws across several republics curbed new West Indian arrivals and prompted partial return migration or internal movement toward the Canal Zone and Pacific plantations [@Gomez2017Extranjero; @Zabaleta2013Mercados].

## Panama's 1903 Separation and the US Panama Canal Zone (1903 to 1979)

Nowhere did international geopolitics intervene more abruptly in Central American demography than on the Panamanian isthmus. During the second half of the nineteenth century, the California Gold Rush (1849), the Panama Railroad (1855) and Ferdinand de Lesseps's ill-fated French canal enterprise (1881 to 1889) brought intermittent bursts of foreign labour and heavy yellow-fever mortality to the Chagres-Panamá corridor [@JaenSuarez1978]. Following the Thousand Days' War in Colombia and the Colombian Senate's rejection of the Hay-Herrán Treaty, Panamanian leaders declared independence on 3 November 1903 with United States naval backing, signing the Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty fifteen days later. That treaty carved a ten-mile-wide strip spanning roughly 1.432 km² across the waist of the new republic—the United States Panama Canal Zone—which operated under US civil and military jurisdiction from 1904 until 1 October 1979 [@JaenSuarez1978; @USCensusCanalZone1973].

Construction of the interoceanic waterway between 1904 and 1914 triggered the largest concentrated labour mobilisation in isthmian history. Sanitation campaigns led by William Gorgas eradicated yellow fever and sharply curtailed malaria, allowing the Isthmian Canal Commission to import more than 45.000 contract labourers, predominantly from Barbados and Jamaica alongside Spanish, Italian and Greek workers—a demographic infusion whose lasting imprint remains clearly detectable in modern Panamanian Y-chromosomal ancestry studies [@Grugni2015Exploring; @JaenSuarez1978]. The special 1912 Canal Zone census counted 62.810 (62,8k) residents living inside the Zone's work camps and administrative towns, led by Gatún (8,9k), Empire (7,2k), Culebra (5,6k), Cristóbal (3,4k), Paraíso (3,2k), Ancón (2,7k), Pedro Miguel (2,6k) and Balboa (1,3k) [@USCensusCanalZone1973]. Once the canal opened in August 1914 and excavation crews dispersed—many settling permanently in the adjacent Panamanian terminal cities of Ciudad de Panamá (rising from 37,5k in 1911 to 59,5k in 1920) and Colón (17,7k to 31,2k)—the Zone's enumerated population contracted sharply to 22.858 (22,9k) in 1920 [@USCensusCanalZone1973; @INECPanama2023]. Subsequent strategic garrisoning during the 1930s, World War II and the early Cold War lifted the Canal Zone back to 39,5k in 1930, 51,8k in 1940 and 52,8k in 1950 before stabilising at 42,1k in 1960 and 44,2k in 1970, clustered around Balboa (2,6k), Gamboa (2,1k), Paraíso (1,7k), Margarita (1,4k), Pedro Miguel (1,4k), Coco Solo (1,2k) and Ancón (1,1k) [@USCensusCanalZone1973]. When the Torrijos-Carter Treaties abolished the Canal Zone in October 1979 and returned the territory to Panamanian sovereignty (with full canal transfer completed on 31 December 1999), the former restricted strip opened rapidly to metropolitan housing, port logistics and suburban spill-over linking Ciudad de Panamá, Arraiján, La Chorrera and Colón [@INECPanama2023; @Maria2017Central].

## British Honduras to Independent Belize: Hurricane Hattie and Belmopan

At the northern Caribbean corner of the isthmus, British Honduras followed a distinct colonial and post-colonial demographic path. Dependent on mahogany and logwood extraction during the nineteenth century, the colony remained tiny—5,2k inhabitants around 1821 and 31,5k in the 1891 census—augmented mid-century by Yucatec Maya and mestizo refugees fleeing Mexico's Caste War of Yucatán (1847 to 1855) into Corozal and Orange Walk, alongside Garifuna settlements in southern Stann Creek (Dangriga) and Toledo [@SIBBelize2024; @HallPerezBrignoli2003]. Well into the mid-twentieth century, demographic weight remained heavily concentrated on the low-lying coastal peninsula of Belize City, which grew from 6,97k in 1891 to 21,9k in 1946 and 32,9k in 1960, holding over a third of the entire colony's 90k residents.

On 31 October 1961, Hurricane Hattie struck Belize City with a catastrophic storm surge that wrecked much of the low-lying wooden capital and exposed the existential vulnerability of concentrating national administration at sea level. In response, the government planned a new inland capital 80 km up the Belize River valley in Cayo District. Formally inaugurated in 1970, Belmopan started with just 274 enumerated inhabitants in the 1970 census and grew slowly during its first two decades (2,9k in 1980 and 3,6k in 1991), even as Belize achieved full independence from the United Kingdom in September 1981 [@SIBBelize2024]. Only after 2000 did administrative expansion, university development and internal migration from neighbouring Guatemala and El Salvador accelerate inland urbanisation: Belmopan multiplied more than fourfold from 5,1k in 2000 to 20,8k in the 2022 census (22,6k projected in 2025), while San Ignacio-Santa Elena reached 21,1k and Cayo District (99,1k) nearly drew level with coastal Belize District (113,6k) within a national population of 397,5k in 2022 [@SIBBelize2024].

## Post-1950 Mortality Decline, Divergent Transitions and Conflict Shocks

The defining demographic rupture of modern Central America began around 1945 to 1955. Public-health campaigns—DDT malaria eradication, vaccination drives, antibiotics, clean drinking water and expanded rural clinics—cut crude death rates and infant mortality precipitously across every republic while birth rates initially stayed above 40 to 45 per 1.000 [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Glei2019Costa]. Aggregate isthmian population, which had taken over a century to rise from 1,17M in 1830 to 9,19M in 1950, surged to 16,21M by 1970, 27,09M by 1990 and 45,27M by 2025—a nearly fivefold multiplication in seventy-five years.

Beneath that shared post-war boom, however, the seven nations diverged dramatically along three demographic pathways. First, Costa Rica—followed closely by Panama—pioneered one of the fastest demographic transitions in Latin America. Aided by universal social security (*Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social*), rural primary healthcare, high female literacy and the abolition of its standing army in 1948, Costa Rica slashed infant and adult mortality to Western European levels after 1950 [@Glei2019Costa; @PerezBrignoli2010] and drove total fertility downward at historic speed from the early 1960s onward [@B2009Presentacion]. Smaller family sizes lifted school attainment across cohorts [@Contributors2014Declining], while regional longevity clusters such as the Nicoya Peninsula attracted global attention before late-born cohorts began converging toward national averages [@Contributors2023Vanishing]. By the 2020s, Costa Rica's sub-replacement fertility left it facing rapid population ageing and rising pension and healthcare fiscal pressures [@Reyestagle2026Fiscal; @INECCostaRica2023].

Second, Guatemala and Honduras maintained high fertility far longer, especially across indigenous rural departments of Guatemala's western highlands and Alta Verapaz and across Honduras's interior hills. Guatemala's national census total expanded from 2,79M in 1950 to 11,24M in 2002 and 14,90M in 2018 (projected past 17M to 18M by 2025), while Honduras grew from 1,37M in 1950 to 6,54M in 2001 and 8,30M in 2013 [@INEGuatemala2019; @INEHonduras2015]. Third, acute geopolitical violence and agrarian land hunger stamped lasting scars onto El Salvador, Nicaragua and Guatemala between 1969 and 1996. In El Salvador, intense rural overcrowding pushed roughly 300k landless Salvadorans across the border into Honduras during the 1950s and 1960s; Honduras's abrupt expulsion of Salvadoran settlers sparked the July 1969 war and closed the regional safety valve [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Gomez2017Extranjero]. When full-scale civil war erupted in El Salvador (1979 to 1992), combat mortality, depressed child survival and mass flight to the United States drained well over half a million citizens, checking national growth and reshaping domestic politics and household remittance dependence for decades [@Rosas1988Mortalidad; @Acevedo2024Emigration]. Nicaragua endured the devastating December 1972 Managua earthquake, the 1978 to 1979 insurrection against Somoza and the 1980s Contra conflict, which stalled child-mortality gains and displaced hundreds of thousands toward Costa Rica and the United States [@Rosas1988Mortalidadb; @Barahona2006Familias; @Zabaleta2013Mercados]. Guatemala's 36-year internal armed conflict (1960 to 1996), peaking in scorched-earth counter-insurgency campaigns across Quiché, Huehuetenango, Alta Verapaz and Petén during 1981 to 1983, killed an estimated 200k people and displaced over a million internally and into southern Mexico [@INEGuatemala2019]. Compounding these shocks, reproductive-health restrictions and maternal mortality disparities across Nicaragua and El Salvador slowed post-war convergence in maternal and infant survival [@Bolanos2013Aborto].

# Methodology

## Territorial Partition into Eight Political Sub-Regions

To capture both sovereign national trajectories and the distinctive enclave geography of the interoceanic transit strip without distorting border counts, JAGUAR partitions the Central American isthmus into eight discrete sub-regions spanning a harmonised 5-arcminute raster footprint of 587.326 km². Six sub-regions correspond directly to modern sovereign states: Guatemala (132.086 km² raster footprint), Belize (British Honduras, 30.074 km²), El Salvador (24.110 km²), Honduras (117.693 km²), Nicaragua (134.545 km²) and Costa Rica (58.031 km²). Panama is deliberately split into two complementary spatial masks: the **Panama Canal Zone (1903 to 1979 OHM Footprint)** (2.967 km² across 35 raster pixels capturing the historic ten-mile trans-isthmian corridor plus bordering terminal-city pixels) and **Panama Republic (excl. Canal Zone)** (87.820 km² across 1.034 pixels). Separating the Canal Zone prevents the sharp 1912 construction peak (62,8k), 1920 demobilisation trough (22,9k) and 1979 sovereign reversion from being blurred into interior Panamanian provinces, while summing the two Panamanian masks reproduces the full republic across every year from 1830 to 2025 [@JaenSuarez1978; @USCensusCanalZone1973; @INECPanama2023].

## Census Anchoring, Intercensal Interpolation and Raster Kriging

Unlike pre-statistical eras reliant on archaeological proxies, Central America after 1821 belongs squarely to the modern census regime, anchored by serial national enumerations across all seven sovereign jurisdictions plus the United States Decennial Censuses of the Panama Canal Zone [@INEGuatemala2019; @DIGESTYC2024; @INEHonduras2015; @INIDENicaragua2006; @INECCostaRica2023; @INECPanama2023; @SIBBelize2024; @USCensusCanalZone1973]. For each sub-region $r$, continuous annual or decadal headcounts $P_r(t)$ between consecutive census dates $t_1$ and $t_2$ are modelled via exponential intercensal compounding combined with spatially disaggregated population grids:

$$P_r(t) = P_r(t_1) \cdot \exp\left(g_r \cdot (t - t_1)\right), \qquad g_r = \frac{\ln\left(P_r(t_2) / P_r(t_1)\right)}{t_2 - t_1}$$

where $g_r$ denotes the continuous intercensal growth rate per annum. To preserve strict spatial mass conservation across sub-national departments, provinces and districts—such as the 25 sub-national administrative units recorded in the chapter's sub-administrative benchmark table—gridded historical population rasters are calibrated against administrative census totals at each decadal slice from 1830 to 1950 and annually from 1950 to 2025. Where nineteenth-century national censuses suffered irregular intervals or omission of remote indigenous and Caribbean communities (notably in Honduras prior to 1887, Nicaragua prior to 1906 and Guatemala's Petén lowlands), regional totals are reconciled against historical demographic reconstructions and retrospective survey evaluations [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Davidson2002; @PerezBrignoli2010; @Jara2014Calendario; @Gonzalez2022Presentacio].

For any territorial unit of area $A_r$, arithmetic population density $D_r(t) = P_r(t) / A_r$ tracks pressure on arable and urban land, while the rank-size hierarchy of the isthmian urban system is evaluated using a log-linear Zipf specification across the top $k = 180$ settlements out of $N = 469$ catalogued urban places:

$$\ln P_{(i)} = c - \alpha \ln(i) + \varepsilon_i$$

where $P_{(i)}$ is the peak census population of the settlement at rank $i$ and $\alpha$ measures urban concentration ($\alpha \approx 1$ denoting classic rank-size balance across a multi-state urban network, $\alpha > 1$ denoting extreme primacy and $\alpha < 1$ indicating polycentric flattening) [@Maria2017Central].

## Settlement Gazetteer Assembly and Metropolitan Ring Reconciliation

Alongside sub-regional macro-trajectories, JAGUAR assembles an evidence-based gazetteer of `r viscount_fmt_number(n_sett, 0L)` catalogued urban settlements spanning all eight masks and all seven countries: 132 in Guatemala, 65 in El Salvador, 65 in Nicaragua, 61 in Costa Rica, 59 in Honduras, 58 in Panama (including 11 historic US Panama Canal Zone townships) and 29 in Belize. Every entry derives directly from official national statistical censuses or US Canal Zone decennial enumerations, yielding a 0,0% crowd-sourced fallback share across the entire source ledger. Saturation audits across four ingestion waves evaluated 471 candidate settlements, excluding just 2 duplicate aliases within a 25 km reconciliation buffer and lowering marginal wave-4 gain to 0,86%.

A central methodological problem in modern Central American urban demography is administrative fragmentation across metropolitan rings [@Maria2017Central]. Because national censuses report municipal populations (*municipios*, *cantones* or *distritos*) separately from functional urban areas, core capitals such as Ciudad de Guatemala (923,4k in 2018) and San Salvador (316,1k in 2007) appear artificially stagnant or shrinking even as their surrounding metropolitan belts boom. To prevent double-counting while preserving full municipal fidelity, JAGUAR explicitly classifies `r n_suburbs` rapidly growing ring municipalities as independent suburban entries linked to their metropolitan parent—including Mixco (463k in 2018), Villa Nueva (426,3k), Villa Canales (124,7k), Chinautla (105k), Amatitlán (98,2k) and Santa Catarina Pinula (71k) around Ciudad de Guatemala; Soyapango (261,1k in 1992; 241,4k in 2007), Mejicanos (140,8k), Apopa (123,1k), Santa Tecla (108,8k), Delgado (95,6k), Ilopango (88,9k), San Marcos (60k), Antiguo Cuscatlán (33k) and Cuscatancingo (35,1k) around San Salvador; and La Chorrera (206k in 2023) and Arraiján (84,5k) west of Ciudad de Panamá (complementing San Miguelito on the eastern flank at 156,6k in 1980 and over 280k in recent censuses) [@INEGuatemala2019; @DIGESTYC2024; @INECPanama2023; @Maria2017Central].

# Testing and Validation

## Reconciliation Against Official National Censuses and Raster Diagnostics

To verify that harmonised raster totals remain faithful to national statistical records, Table \ref{tab:census-validation} cross-checks JAGUAR's sub-regional raster trajectory against official national census benchmarks from independence through the 2020s [@INEGuatemala2019; @INEHonduras2015; @DIGESTYC2024; @INIDENicaragua2006; @INECCostaRica2023; @INECPanama2023; @SIBBelize2024; @USCensusCanalZone1973]. Across the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, agreement between the harmonised raster model and census enumerations is close across every core republic: Guatemala's raster reaches 16,35M in 2018 (16,25M in 2025) against the official 2018 census of 14,90M (which INE itself noted carried roughly 8% under-enumeration, matching post-census demographic reconciliations near 16,3M); Honduras's raster stands at 8,16M in 2013 (8,27M in 2025) against the official 2013 census of 8,30M; El Salvador's raster reaches 5,78M in 2024 against the official VII Censo of 6,03M; Nicaragua's raster records 5,02M in 2005 (5,43M in 2025) against the official 2005 census of 5,14M; Costa Rica's raster hits 5,18M in 2022 against the official 2022 census of 5,04M; and the two Panamanian masks combine to 3,86M in 2023 (3,87M in 2025) against Panama's official 2023 census of 4,06M.

```{r tab-census-validation, results='asis'}
val_df <- data.frame(
  Jurisdiction = c(
    "Guatemala",
    "Honduras",
    "El Salvador",
    "Nicaragua",
    "Costa Rica",
    "Panama (Republic + Canal Zone)",
    "US Panama Canal Zone (1912-1970)",
    "Belize (British Honduras)"
  ),
  Census1950 = c("2,79M", "1,37M", "1,86M", "1,06M", "800,9k", "805,3k", "52,8k", "68k"),
  Raster1950 = c("3,07M", "1,33M", "1,79M", "1,22M", "817,8k", "901k", "52,8k", "64,6k"),
  LatestCensus = c(
    "14,90M (2018)",
    "8,30M (2013)",
    "6,03M (2024)",
    "5,14M (2005)",
    "5,04M (2022)",
    "4,06M (2023)",
    "44,2k (1970)",
    "397,5k (2022)"
  ),
  RasterMatched = c(
    "16,35M (2018)",
    "8,16M (2013)",
    "5,78M (2024)",
    "5,02M (2005)",
    "5,18M (2022)",
    "3,86M (2023)",
    "44,2k (1970)",
    "498,9k (2022)"
  ),
  Raster2025 = c("16,25M", "8,27M", "5,78M", "5,43M", "5,17M", "3,87M", "567,2k*", "502k"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

viscount_table(
  val_df,
  "Comparison of official national census enumerations against harmonised JAGUAR raster totals at 1950, latest census year and 2025 (*post-1979 Canal Zone footprint reflects reverted Panamanian metropolitan growth).",
  c("Jurisdiction", "1950 Census", "1950 Raster", "Latest Official Census", "Matched Raster", "2025 Raster"),
  list(label = "tab:census-validation", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Three known raster-disaggregation artefacts surface clearly during validation and are documented transparently rather than smoothed away. First, at the 5-arcminute grid resolution (~9 km equatorial pixel width), narrow or small coastal territories absorb boundary-pixel spillover from denser neighbours: Belize's raster registers 63,5k in 1830 and 498,9k in 2022 against official British Honduras and Belize censuses of 5,2k (1821), 31,5k (1891) and 397,5k (2022) [@SIBBelize2024]. Similarly, the 35-pixel Canal Zone mask expands to 2.967 km²—roughly double the historic 1.432 km² treaty strip—because coastal and terminal-city grid cells straddling Ciudad de Panamá and Colón fall inside the pixel mask after 1979. Second, in the nineteenth-century pre-harmonised grid slices, sharp step jumps appear when national census anchors supersede coarse global hindcasts: Guatemala jumps from 368,1k in 1890 to 1,60M in 1900, El Salvador from 207,3k in 1910 to 1,37M in 1920 and Nicaragua from 461,2k in 1920 to 1,12M in 1930. Readers analysing nineteenth-century levels should therefore rely on the direct historical census series (Guatemala 535k in 1821 and 1,36M in 1893; El Salvador 248k in 1821 and 703,5k in 1892; Nicaragua 185k in 1821 and 505,4k in 1906) alongside the post-1930 continuous raster curves [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @INEGuatemala2019; @DIGESTYC2024; @INIDENicaragua2006]. Third, across the US Canal Zone administration window (1910 to 1979), direct decennial census overriding holds the series to exact historical accuracy: 62.810 in 1912, 22.858 in 1920, 39.467 in 1930, 51.827 in 1940, 52.822 in 1950, 42.122 in 1960 and 44.198 in 1970 [@USCensusCanalZone1973].

## Sub-National Administrative Cross-Check

A second independent validation tests spatial concentration inside each republic against 25 leading first-order sub-national census units (departments, provinces and districts) assembled from national statistical institutes and Davidson's historical territorial compilation (Table \ref{tab:hgis-subadmin}) [@INEGuatemala2019; @INEHonduras2015; @DIGESTYC2024; @INIDENicaragua2006; @INECCostaRica2023; @INECPanama2023; @SIBBelize2024; @Davidson2002]. Across every country, the leading metropolitan department or province anchors between 20% and 35% of the national headcount: Guatemala Department holds 3,02M (20,2% of Guatemala's 2018 census), San Salvador Department 1,56M (25,9% of El Salvador's 2024 census), San José Province 1,60M (31,7% of Costa Rica's 2022 census), Panamá Province 1,44M plus Panamá Oeste 653,7k (51,5% combined of Panama's 2023 census), Managua Department 1,26M (24,6% of Nicaragua's 2005 census) and Belize District 113,6k alongside Cayo District 99,1k (53,5% combined of Belize's 2022 census). Only Honduras splits national demographic leadership evenly between two rival poles—industrial Cortés (1,56M in 2013) on the Caribbean Sula plain and administrative Francisco Morazán (1,51M) in the central highlands—confirming the bipolar urban structure captured in our raster and city gazetteer [@INEHonduras2015; @Maria2017Central].

```{r tab-hgis-subadmin, results='asis'}
hgis_rows <- lapply(summary_data$hgis_subadmin_table, function(u) {
  lvl <- paste0(toupper(substring(u$level, 1, 1)), substring(u$level, 2))
  data.frame(
    Unit = clean_label(u$unit_name),
    Country = clean_label(u$country),
    Level = lvl,
    Year = as.character(u$year),
    Pop = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(u$population), 0L),
    Source = clean_hgis_source(u$source, u$country),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_hgis <- do.call(rbind, hgis_rows)
rownames(df_hgis) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_hgis,
  "Leading first-order sub-national administrative census benchmarks across all seven Central American states (25 units).",
  c("Administrative Unit", "Country", "Tier", "Census Year", "Population", "Statistical Source"),
  list(label = "tab:hgis-subadmin", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 30L)
)
```

# Results

## Macro-Regional Demographic Trajectory (1821 to 2025)

Central America's modern demographic history unfolds across three distinct growth epochs visible in Figure \ref{fig:ca-trajectory} and quantified across all eight sub-regions in Table \ref{tab:subregion-trajectories}. During the nineteenth-century post-independence epoch (1821 to 1900), expansion stayed modest under recurring civil wars, epidemic mortality and limited overland transport, lifting the eight-region aggregate from 1,17M in 1830 to 3,40M in 1900 (and roughly 3,8M to 4M using contemporary national censuses). During the early export-modernisation epoch (1900 to 1950), coffee revenues, banana railways, canal sanitation and initial urban waterworks pushed growth rates above 2% per annum, lifting the isthmus nearly threefold to 9,19M by 1950. Finally, during the post-1950 demographic explosion (1950 to 2025), sustained mortality collapse raised the regional total nearly fivefold to 45,27M in 2025—peaking in annual expansion speed during the 1960s and 1970s (3,0% to 3,3% per year) before moderating steadily after 2000 as fertility fell across every state and international emigration siphoned off working-age cohorts [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Maria2017Central; @Gonzalez2022Presentacio].

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/central_american_republics_population_trajectory.png",
  "Population trajectory across Central America and its four most populous republics from 1830 to 2025 (Panel A) and sub-regional population densities in 2025 (Panel B).",
  "fig:ca-trajectory"
)
```

```{r tab-subregion-trajectories, results='asis'}
sub_rows <- lapply(subregions, function(r) {
  tr <- r$trajectory
  area_v <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p1830 <- as.numeric(tr[["1830"]])
  p1900 <- as.numeric(tr[["1900"]])
  p1950 <- as.numeric(tr[["1950"]])
  p1980 <- as.numeric(tr[["1980"]])
  p2000 <- as.numeric(tr[["2000"]])
  p2025 <- as.numeric(tr[["2025"]])
  d2025 <- as.numeric(r$end_density_km2)
  data.frame(
    Subregion = clean_label(r$name),
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(round(area_v), 0L),
    P1830 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1830),
    P1900 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1900),
    P1950 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1950),
    P1980 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1980),
    P2000 = viscount_fmt_pop(p2000),
    P2025 = viscount_fmt_pop(p2025),
    Dens2025 = viscount_fmt_number(d2025, 1L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sub <- do.call(rbind, sub_rows)
df_sub_tot <- data.frame(
  Subregion = "Isthmian Total (8 Sub-Regions)",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(round(tot_area), 0L),
  P1830 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1830),
  P1900 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1900),
  P1950 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1950),
  P1980 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1980),
  P2000 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_2000),
  P2025 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_2025),
  Dens2025 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_2025 / tot_area, 1L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_sub <- rbind(df_sub, df_sub_tot)
rownames(df_sub) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_sub,
  "Harmonised sub-regional population trajectories (1830 to 2025), raster footprint areas and 2025 arithmetic densities (inhabitants per km²) across Central America.",
  c("Sub-Region", "Area (km²)", "1830", "1900", "1950", "1980", "2000", "2025", "2025 Dens."),
  list(label = "tab:subregion-trajectories", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Regional Divergence: Highland Primacy, Pacific Density and Atlantic Frontiers

Across the two centuries since independence, national shares of Central America's population shifted notably as fertility transitions, land availability and emigration interacted. Guatemala remained the demographic giant throughout, rising from 535k at independence and 1,36M in 1893 to 3,07M (raster) in 1950, 6,59M in 1980, 11,47M in 2000 and 16,25M in 2025 (35,9% of the entire isthmus, 123 inhabitants per km²) [@INEGuatemala2019]. Unlike neighbouring republics that urbanised rapidly into single coastal corridors, Guatemala preserved deep highland rural density across western Maya departments—Alta Verapaz (1,22M in 2018), Huehuetenango (1,17M) and San Marcos (1,03M)—while its metropolitan valley around Ciudad de Guatemala (3,02M department total) spilled heavily into Mixco (463k), Villa Nueva (426,3k), San Juan Sacatepéquez (156k) and Villa Canales (124,7k) alongside regional highland and piedmont centres such as Cobán (212k), Quetzaltenango (180,7k), Jalapa (159,8k) and Escuintla (156,3k) [@INEGuatemala2019; @Maria2017Central].

Honduras climbed into second place demographically during the late twentieth century, expanding more than sixfold after 1950 from 1,33M to 3,28M in 1980, 6,25M in 2000 and 8,27M in 2025 (18,3% of the isthmus, 70,2 inhabitants per km²; official 2013 census 8,30M) [@INEHonduras2015]. Its growth reflects a pronounced northward spatial tilt: whereas nineteenth-century Honduras centred on the colonial silver and cattle valleys of Comayagua (8,5k in 1850) and Tegucigalpa (10k in 1850) [@Davidson2002], twentieth-century banana railways and post-1980 *maquila* apparel manufacturing shifted economic gravity to the Sula Valley. By 2023, San Pedro Sula (701,2k) and adjacent Choloma (220,3k), Villanueva and La Lima formed an industrial conurbation rivaling highland Tegucigalpa (1,13M), while the Caribbean port of La Ceiba reached 209k and interior agricultural hubs such as El Progreso, Comayagua (120,5k), Choluteca, Danlí and Juticalpa anchored secondary trade networks [@INEHonduras2015; @Maria2017Central].

El Salvador presents the sharpest contrast between extreme spatial density and emigration-capped growth. At 239,9 inhabitants per km² across its raster footprint (and over 280 inhabitants per km² on its 21.041 km² official land area), El Salvador sits atop the isthmian density ranking (Figure \ref{fig:ca-trajectory}, Panel B), nearly double Guatemala and fourteen times Belize [@DIGESTYC2024]. Expanding rapidly from 1,79M in 1950 to 4,05M in 1980, Salvadoran demographic momentum decelerated abruptly during the 1980s civil war and subsequent post-war emigration to North America, crawling from 5,27M in 2000 to 5,78M in 2025 (official 2024 census 6,03M) [@DIGESTYC2024; @Acevedo2024Emigration; @Rosas1988Mortalidad]. Inside the country, San Salvador proper peaked at 415,3k in 1992 and eased to 316,1k in 2007 as households spread across ring municipalities—Soyapango (261,1k in 1992; 241,4k in 2007), Mejicanos (140,8k), Apopa (123,1k), Santa Tecla (108,8k), Delgado (95,6k) and Ilopango (88,9k)—while western coffee capital Santa Ana (198,3k) and eastern hub San Miguel (156k) anchored regional catchments [@DIGESTYC2024; @Maria2017Central].

Nicaragua's demographic arc moved from 1,22M in 1950 to 2,60M in 1980, 4,64M in 2000 and 5,43M in 2025 (40,4 inhabitants per km²; official 2005 census 5,14M) [@INIDENicaragua2006]. Historically split between rival colonial towns León (25k in 1850; 177,3k in 2023) and Granada (15k in 1850; 106,7k in 2023), Nicaragua consolidated around its compromise capital of Managua (chosen in 1852), which surged from 12k in 1850 and 109,4k in 1950 to 384,9k in 1971—just months before the December 1972 earthquake levelled its central core—and 1,06M by 2023, flanked by suburban satellites Tipitapa (150,6k) and Ciudad Sandino alongside Pacific agricultural cities Masaya (140,7k), Chinandega, Matagalpa and Estelí [@INIDENicaragua2006; @Barahona2006Familias]. Yet despite wide open plains along the Caribbean autonomous regions (anchored by Puerto Cabezas at 86,3k and Bluefields at 56,4k), conflict displacement in the 1980s and recurring labour emigration to Costa Rica and the United States kept Nicaragua's density low [@Rosas1988Mortalidadb; @Zabaleta2013Mercados; @Bolanos2013Aborto].

## Early Demographic Transition in Costa Rica and Trans-Isthmian Panama

Southern Central America illustrates the opposite pole of isthmian demography: sustained social investment, rapid fertility decline and strong immigration attraction. Costa Rica multiplied more than sixfold after 1950 from 817,8k to 2,28M in 1980, 3,91M in 2000 and 5,17M in 2025 (89,1 inhabitants per km²; official 2022 census 5,04M), bolstered after 1980 by hundreds of thousands of Nicaraguan migrants working in construction, agriculture and domestic services [@INECCostaRica2023; @PerezBrignoli2010; @Zabaleta2013Mercados]. Having driven total fertility from over 6,5 children per woman in 1960 down toward 1,3 to 1,5 by the early 2020s while achieving life expectancies near 80 years, Costa Rica's population plateaued around 5,17M to 5,18M between 2022 and 2025 and now confronts rapid workforce ageing [@B2009Presentacion; @Glei2019Costa; @Contributors2014Declining; @Contributors2023Vanishing; @Reyestagle2026Fiscal]. Spatially, its Greater Metropolitan Area (*Gran Área Metropolitana*) fuses four colonial Central Valley cores—San José (1,45M urban agglomeration in 2020), Heredia (367,9k), Cartago (232,3k) and Alajuela (196,9k)—leaving Pacific Puntarenas (87,5k), Atlantic Limón (65,3k) and Guanacaste's Liberia (59,1k) as secondary regional nodes [@INECCostaRica2023; @Maria2017Central].

Panama followed a closely parallel trajectory shaped by its interoceanic service economy. Excluding the Canal Zone, Panama Republic climbed from 848,1k in 1950 to 1,72M in 1980, 2,26M in 2000 and 3,30M in 2025 (37,6 inhabitants per km²), while the reverted Canal Zone corridor surged from 44,2k under US governance in 1970 to 287,9k in 1980, 467k in 2000 and 567,2k in 2025 (191,2 inhabitants per km²—second only to El Salvador in sub-regional density) [@INECPanama2023; @USCensusCanalZone1973; @JaenSuarez1978]. Combined, Panama reached 4,06M in its 2023 census, with more than half of all citizens concentrated in the trans-isthmian corridor spanning Ciudad de Panamá (1,13M), San Miguelito, La Chorrera (206k), Arraiján (84,5k) and Colón (159,2k), leaving Chiriquí's David (103,9k) and the Azuero towns of Chitré (57,4k) and Santiago de Veraguas (51,3k) as the main interior centres [@INECPanama2023; @Grugni2015Exploring]. At the far northern Caribbean corner, Belize remained the least densely peopled territory on the isthmus at 16,7 inhabitants per km² on the raster footprint (17,3 on its official 22.966 km² land area at 397,5k in 2022), yet its steady inland shift toward Belmopan (20,8k) and San Ignacio (21,1k) alongside northern Orange Walk (14,6k) and coastal San Pedro (15,5k) gradually balanced Belize City's long colonial dominance [@SIBBelize2024].

## Urbanisation, Rank-Size Structure and Metropolitan Rings

Between 1950 and 2025, Central America crossed decisively from a rural agrarian isthmus—less than 30% urban at mid-century—to a majority-urban corridor approaching 60% overall and exceeding 70% in Costa Rica, El Salvador and Panama [@Maria2017Central]. Figure \ref{fig:ca-hierarchy} maps both the upper urban tier and the cross-national rank-size distribution across all 469 catalogued settlements. Remarkably, because the isthmus is divided among seven sovereign republics—each cultivating its own primate capital—the combined Central American urban system produces a tightly balanced, near-Zipfian rank-size slope ($\alpha = 0,92$, $R^2 = 0,98$ across the top 180 settlements), avoiding the extreme single-city skew typical of individual national systems [@Maria2017Central].

```{r fig-hierarchy, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/central_american_republics_urban_hierarchy.png",
  "Twelve largest catalogued Central American urban settlements by peak census population (Panel A) and log-log rank-size distribution across 469 settlements showing a near-Zipfian power-law fit ($\\alpha = 0,92$, $R^2 = 0,98$, Panel B), 1821 to 2025.",
  "fig:ca-hierarchy"
)
```

Table \ref{tab:top-cities} presents the 25 largest urban settlements in the isthmian gazetteer alongside historic Canal Zone administration centres, illustrating how national capitals, industrial port hubs and independent ring suburbs interlock across the urban hierarchy. Four national metropolitan cores top one million inhabitants in their peak census series: San José (1,45M urban agglomeration in 2020), Ciudad de Panamá (1,13M in 2023), Tegucigalpa (1,13M in 2023) and Managua (1,06M in 2023), with Ciudad de Guatemala proper at 942,3k in 2002 (923,4k in 2018) rising past 2,2M once its directly contiguous ring municipalities of Mixco (463k), Villa Nueva (426,3k), San Juan Sacatepéquez (156k), Villa Canales (124,7k), Chinautla (105k) and Amatitlán (98,2k) are combined [@INEGuatemala2019; @Maria2017Central]. Similarly, San Salvador proper (415,3k in 1992; 316,1k in 2007) sits at the core of a continuous metropolitan ring anchored by Soyapango (261,1k), Mejicanos (140,8k), Apopa (123,1k) and Santa Tecla (108,8k), while Ciudad de Panamá expands westward into La Chorrera (206k) and Arraiján (84,5k) and eastward across San Miguelito (156,6k in 1980) [@DIGESTYC2024; @INECPanama2023].

```{r tab-top-cities, results='asis'}
all_list <- lapply(names(sett_data), function(k) {
  e <- sett_data[[k]]
  pvals <- as.numeric(unlist(e$population))
  pyrs <- as.integer(names(e$population))
  idx_pk <- which.max(pvals)
  list(
    key = k,
    name = clean_label(e$name),
    country = clean_label(e$country),
    region = if (e$region_id %in% names(reg_lookup)) reg_lookup[[e$region_id]] else clean_label(e$region_id),
    scope = if (identical(e$population_scope, "suburb")) "Independent suburb" else "City proper",
    first_yr = min(pyrs),
    last_yr = max(pyrs),
    peak_pop = pvals[idx_pk],
    peak_yr = pyrs[idx_pk]
  )
})
ord_idx <- order(vapply(all_list, function(x) x$peak_pop, numeric(1)), decreasing = TRUE)
top25 <- all_list[ord_idx[seq_len(25L)]]

cz_keys <- c("Gatún-Panama", "Balboa-Panama", "Gamboa-Panama", "Cristóbal-Panama", "Ancón-Panama")
cz_items <- Filter(function(x) x$key %in% cz_keys, all_list)
cz_items <- cz_items[order(vapply(cz_items, function(x) x$peak_pop, numeric(1)), decreasing = TRUE)]
disp_list <- c(top25, cz_items)

city_rows <- lapply(disp_list, function(x) {
  data.frame(
    Settlement = x$name,
    Country = x$country,
    Scope = x$scope,
    Span = paste0(x$first_yr, " to ", x$last_yr),
    PeakPop = viscount_fmt_pop(x$peak_pop),
    PeakYr = as.character(x$peak_yr),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_cities <- do.call(rbind, city_rows)
rownames(df_cities) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_cities,
  "Top 25 Central American urban settlements (including independent metropolitan suburbs Mixco, Villa Nueva, Soyapango, La Chorrera and San Miguelito) plus five historic US Panama Canal Zone townships, 1821 to 2025.",
  c("Settlement", "Country", "Administrative Scope", "Census Span", "Peak Pop.", "Peak Year"),
  list(label = "tab:top-cities", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 32L)
)
```

# Limitations

Five structural constraints govern the interpretation of modern Central American census reconstructions.

First, national census calendars across the seven republics are asynchronous and suffered lengthy wartime or budgetary interruptions. Nicaragua has not published a full population census since 2005 [@INIDENicaragua2006], Honduras last completed one in 2013 [@INEHonduras2015] and El Salvador went seventeen years between 2007 and 2024 [@DIGESTYC2024]. Post-2013 Honduran and post-2005 Nicaraguan figures therefore depend on official intercensal projections and vital-register updates rather than fresh house-to-house enumerations, widening uncertainty over recent emigration flows [@Zabaleta2013Mercados; @Gonzalez2022Presentacio].

Second, nineteenth-century enumerations prior to 1880 suffered severe under-registration across dispersed indigenous highlands (Guatemala's Quiché, Huehuetenango and Alta Verapaz), remote Caribbean rain forests (Honduran and Nicaraguan Mosquitia, Panamanian Darién) and itinerant timber camps in British Honduras [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @Davidson2002]. Even in modern enumerations, coverage shortfalls persist: Guatemala's 2018 census (14,90M enumerated) and Costa Rica's 2022 census (5,04M) experienced elevated non-response in gated urban neighbourhoods and remote rural districts, creating a documented 5% to 9% gap between raw enumerated counts and demographic reconciliation totals [@INEGuatemala2019; @INECCostaRica2023].

Third, spatial rasterisation at 5-arcminute resolution (~9 km pixel width) introduces measurable boundary-pixel leakage for narrow or compact jurisdictions. As documented in Table \ref{tab:census-validation}, Belize's raster footprint (30.074 km² vs 22.966 km² official land area) absorbs adjacent Petén and Quintana Roo border pixels, lifting its 2022 raster estimate to 498,9k against the 397,5k SIB census [@SIBBelize2024], while the 35-pixel Panama Canal Zone mask (2.967 km² vs 1.432 km² historic treaty strip) captures parts of adjacent Ciudad de Panamá and Colón after 1979 reversion. Furthermore, pre-1930 grid slices exhibit sharp upward steps in 1900 (Guatemala), 1920 (El Salvador) and 1930 (Nicaragua) where national census constraints supersede sparser nineteenth-century hindcasts.

Fourth, definitions of urban settlements vary widely across national statistical offices. Costa Rica's INEC reports metropolitan urban agglomerations around San José (1,45M), Heredia (367,9k) and Cartago (232,3k) that incorporate contiguous suburban cantons, whereas Guatemala's INE and El Salvador's DIGESTYC/ONEC tabulate strict municipal boundaries (*municipios*), splitting functional conurbations across core capitals and independent suburban municipalities such as Mixco, Villa Nueva, Soyapango and Mejicanos [@Maria2017Central; @INECCostaRica2023; @INEGuatemala2019; @DIGESTYC2024]. Cross-country comparisons of single-city rankings must always keep this municipal-versus-agglomeration distinction in view.

Fifth, irregular international migration—especially from El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua to the United States, Mexico and Costa Rica since 1979—escapes full capture in origin-country civil registers [@Acevedo2024Emigration; @Zabaleta2013Mercados; @Jara2014Calendario]. Rapid surges in emigration during the 1980s civil wars and the post-2014 northern-triangle migration waves cause intercensal projections to overshoot actual resident populations until corrected by subsequent census rounds, as confirmed by El Salvador's 2024 enumeration of 6,03M against earlier projections exceeding 6,6M [@DIGESTYC2024].

# Conclusion

Over the two centuries from 1821 to 2025, Central America evolved from a lightly settled post-colonial bridge of roughly 1,2M inhabitants into a complex, predominantly urban region of 45,27M people spanning seven sovereign nations. Political fragmentation after the dissolution of the Federal Republic of Central America in 1841, the loss of Chiapas to Mexico in 1824, the consolidation of British Honduras and the 1903 creation of Panama and its US-administered Canal Zone ensured that no single metropolis or uniform demographic regime ever dominated the isthmus [@HallPerezBrignoli2003; @JaenSuarez1978]. Instead, nineteenth-century coffee monocultures packed highland and Pacific slopes from Guatemala to Costa Rica, while twentieth-century banana railways and interoceanic canal construction opened the Atlantic littoral through West Indian labour migration and forged a unique trans-isthmian enclave that returned to Panamanian sovereignty in 1979 [@USCensusCanalZone1973; @Grugni2015Exploring].

After 1950, rapid public-health gains unleashed an extraordinary demographic expansion that multiplied isthmian population nearly fivefold in seventy-five years before fracturing along divergent socio-political lines. Costa Rica and Panama completed rapid fertility transitions and entered twenty-first-century demographic ageing [@Glei2019Costa; @B2009Presentacion; @Reyestagle2026Fiscal]; Guatemala and Honduras sustained vigorous rural and industrial population growth well into the 2010s [@INEGuatemala2019; @INEHonduras2015]; Belize gradually rebalanced away from hurricane-prone Belize City toward inland Belmopan and Cayo [@SIBBelize2024]; and El Salvador and Nicaragua saw intense twentieth-century conflicts and sustained emigration check domestic growth while leaving El Salvador the most densely settled republic on the American mainland [@Acevedo2024Emigration; @Barahona2006Familias; @DIGESTYC2024]. Taken together, the harmonised sub-regional rasters, 25 first-order administrative benchmarks and 469-settlement urban gazetteer establish a unified quantitative ledger for modern Central American population history.

# Appendix

## Historic US Panama Canal Zone Townships (1912 to 1970)

Table \ref{tab:canal-zone-towns} documents the complete decennial census trajectory of the 11 historic townships enumerated inside the United States Panama Canal Zone from the 1912 construction-peak census through the final US decennial enumeration in 1970 [@USCensusCanalZone1973]. The series captures the rapid evaporation of massive excavation camps such as Empire (7,2k in 1912) and Culebra (5,6k in 1912) following the opening of the waterway in 1914, contrasted with the durable administrative and operational communities at Balboa, Gamboa, Paraíso, Margarita, Pedro Miguel, Coco Solo, Ancón, Cristóbal and Gatún.

```{r tab-canal-zone-towns, results='asis'}
cz_entries <- Filter(function(e) {
  any(grepl("Panama Canal Zone", unlist(e$sources), fixed = TRUE))
}, sett_data)

cz_rows <- lapply(cz_entries, function(e) {
  pop <- e$population
  get_y <- function(y) {
    val <- pop[[as.character(y)]]
    if (is.null(val)) "-" else viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(val), 0L)
  }
  pvals <- as.numeric(unlist(pop))
  data.frame(
    Township = clean_label(e$name),
    Y1912 = get_y(1912),
    Y1920 = get_y(1920),
    Y1930 = get_y(1930),
    Y1940 = get_y(1940),
    Y1950 = get_y(1950),
    Y1960 = get_y(1960),
    Y1970 = get_y(1970),
    Peak = max(pvals),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_cz <- do.call(rbind, cz_rows)
df_cz <- df_cz[order(df_cz$Peak, decreasing = TRUE), ]
df_cz$Peak <- NULL
rownames(df_cz) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_cz,
  "Decennial population enumerations of 11 US Panama Canal Zone townships from the 1912 construction peak to 1970 (U.S. Bureau of the Census).",
  c("Canal Zone Township", "1912", "1920", "1930", "1940", "1950", "1960", "1970"),
  list(label = "tab:canal-zone-towns", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## National Gazetteer Distribution and Provenance Summary

Table \ref{tab:country-gazetteer} summarises the national distribution of all 469 catalogued Central American settlements, contrasting city-proper municipal cores (`r as.integer(summary_data$settlement_stats$city_proper_count)`) with independently reconciled suburban municipalities (`r n_suburbs`) across all seven states.

```{r tab-country-gazetteer, results='asis'}
countries <- c("Guatemala", "El Salvador", "Nicaragua", "Costa Rica", "Honduras", "Panama", "Belize")
cty_rows <- lapply(countries, function(cn) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e$country, cn), sett_data)
  n_tot <- length(sub_e)
  n_sub <- sum(vapply(sub_e, function(e) identical(e$population_scope, "suburb"), logical(1)))
  n_core <- n_tot - n_sub
  pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e$population))), numeric(1))
  idx_m <- which.max(pks)
  lead <- paste0(clean_label(sub_e[[idx_m]]$name), " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  data.frame(
    Country = cn,
    Total = viscount_fmt_number(n_tot, 0L),
    Core = viscount_fmt_number(n_core, 0L),
    Suburbs = viscount_fmt_number(n_sub, 0L),
    Share = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * n_tot / n_sett, 1L), "%"),
    Lead = lead,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_cty <- do.call(rbind, cty_rows)
rownames(df_cty) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_cty,
  "National breakdown of 469 catalogued Central American settlements by administrative scope and leading recorded city, 1821 to 2025.",
  c("Country", "Total Sites", "City Proper", "Suburbs", "Share", "Leading Recorded City (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:country-gazetteer", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

1. Historical census figures for Chiapas (detached to Mexico in 1824) are excluded from the Central American regional total throughout 1821 to 2025 and accounted within JAGUAR's Mexican national chapter to guarantee strict continental mass conservation across Mesoamerica.
2. Raster footprint areas reported in Table \ref{tab:subregion-trajectories} reflect 5-arcminute equal-area pixel masks (587.326 km² total) rather than vector cadastral land areas (~521.876 km² across the seven sovereign states), explaining the modest upward area buffer along intricate Caribbean cays, gulfs and coastal borders.
3. Because Costa Rica's INEC publishes metropolitan urban agglomeration totals for San José, Heredia, Cartago and Alajuela from 2000 onward while Guatemala's INE and El Salvador's DIGESTYC/BCR-ONEC publish municipal city-proper counts separately from ring suburbs, direct inter-city comparisons in Table \ref{tab:top-cities} explicitly flag administrative scope.
